title: Quote Tweets: the nerds who willed a feature into being
summary:
The most quotable take is Visakan Veerasamy (@visakanv) calling quote tweets a “killer feature” and basically yelling: stop burying them in the notification sludge—give QTs their own tab and treat them like first-class infrastructure (“likes, RTs, QTs”). What starts as a UX gripe (“losing track of QTs breaks my user experience”) quickly turns into a bigger theory of Twitter-as-knowledge-machine: QTs let you do “threads in reverse,” where multiple people build different paths that all point to the same tweet, like a messy but real bidirectional idea graph.

Arc-wise: it kicks off with early “this exists” history (Igor Brigadir noting “Retweet With Comment” in 2015 and how it kills subtweeting by notifying the target). The 2019 peak is Visa’s viral push + Malcolm Ocean (@Malcolm_Ocean) amplifying it into a design philosophy—Twitter accidentally being the best “interactive reading” tool, and QTs being the link mechanism that makes collective sensemaking possible. Then Malcolm goes full power-user-political-organizer and literally ships a hack: a JavaScript console script that filters notifications to simulate a QT tab, proving both demand and how broken the native UI was.

The victory lap hits in 2020 when Patrick McKenzie (@patio11) celebrates Twitter finally adding “view quote retweets” without needing weird search kung fu—validation that the obsessive lobbying worked. After that, the discourse mutates into a wishlist and then a sequel: Qiaochu Yuan (@QiaochuYuan) says the move is to “talk obsessively… until they add them,” and pivots to campaigning for multi-QTs (quote 2–4 tweets at once) because screenshots are a dead-end (no links, no search, no backlinks). The energy fades into frustration again in 2023 when X buries/partially breaks QT backlink visibility (“this breaks QT-backlinking!”), and ends on Visa’s 2024 poetic closure: one of Twitter’s best decisions was “allow us to put tweets inside other tweets”—nested sanctums, nested ideas, nested systems.

Why care: because this is the rare thread where platform “discourse” actually cashes a check—users articulated a concrete feature need, built hacks around it, and got the product to shift. And the deeper point is uncomfortable: Twitter’s real superpower wasn’t hot takes, it was the linking—QTs as the smallest unit of collaborative knowledge-building. When that gets hidden or broken, the whole “collective consciousness” vibe collapses back into isolated posts.
